newsitem.title: JAPAN: INTERVIEW - Argentina may see lower rates - minister.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Argentina may see lower rates - minister.

text.p: Argentine Economy Minister Roque Fernandez said on Monday that an upgrading of the nation's foreign currency debt will help lower domestic interest rates in the near term.

Fernandez told Reuters Financial Television in Tokyo that an upgrading of Argentina's $62.2 billion long-term foreign currency debt to BB from BB minus by rating agency Standard and Poor's Corp was something that had already been anticipated by the markets.

"We believe that the upgrading, in a way, was catching up with what was already being observed in international markets. These will consolidate the downward trend in interest rates, so we expect that to be important for investment in Argentina," Fernandez said.

Asked whether there could be a credit easing in the near term, the Argentine minister said: "Yes, I think that the dynamics we have been observing in the past -- new flows of funds going into Argentina with longer maturity -- that will prevail in the future again."
Just before the United States raised its federal funds rate by 25 basis points, Fernandez had said a rise in U.S. interest rates would produce an immediate increase in interest rates in Argentina.

In Monday's interview, Fernandez also gave an upbeat assessment of the Argentine economy, saying the country was likely to achieve higher economic growth than the original government forecast of five percent gross domestic product (GDP) growth for 1997.
"Five percent is highly conservative. We could be higher than that," he said.
He did not think that new import financing rules by Brazil would "very seriously" affect Argentina's exports, but said that more time was needed before making a concrete assessment.

Argentina and other Mercosur partners have been complaining about new limits imposed by Brazil on import financing. But they were able to strike an agreement last week to make the regulations a touch more flexible for goods from the trade bloc for 120 days before a long-term solution is found.

Fernandez said he did not think Brazil would devalue its currency to reduce its trade deficit, since modifying foreign exchange rates alone would not solve the problem and could threaten the stability of the currency.
Rather, Brazil is trying to attack the fiscal deficit problem by implementing a privatisation programme which will help cancel out foreign debt, Fernandez said.
"If these measures are taken, (the) current account situation will improve for Brazil," he said.
